extraction.name: Natural Questions
extraction.description: A question answering dataset pairing real anonymized, aggregated Google Search queries with Wikipedia pages, where annotators label long answers, short answers, or null.
extraction.creator: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, Slav Petrov
extraction.citeAs: Kwiatkowski, Tom, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, and Slav Petrov. 2019. "Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research." Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics 7: 453–466. https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00276
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were sampled from anonymized, aggregated Google Search queries using heuristics, then paired with a Wikipedia page appearing in the top 5 search results. Human annotators labeled question quality, long answers, and short answers using a custom interface.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Examples may have no answer labeled; 51% of examples have no long answer, and annotators can mark null when no viable candidate exists on the Wikipedia page.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real anonymized, aggregated Google Search queries and Wikipedia pages returned in the top 5 Google search results.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Simple heuristics were used to filter the query stream to retain likely factual questions of 8 words or more, and only queries with a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results were kept.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries were filtered by heuristic rules to remove many non-questions and focus on longer factual questions; questions were retained only if a Wikipedia page appeared in the top 5 search results. Part-of-speech tags and entities were identified using Google's Cloud NLP API.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators used a three-stage process: determine whether the question is good or bad, select the earliest HTML bounding box containing enough information as the long answer or mark no answer, and then select entity spans, yes/no, or no short answer within the long answer.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was monitored and evaluated using post hoc expert judgments and k-way annotations. The paper reports 25-way annotations on a subset to study variability and disagreement, and defines expert categories Correct, Correct but debatable, and Wrong.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 for training examples; 5 for development and test examples; 25 on a 302-example subset for variability analysis
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: A pool of around 50 annotators; four experts who prepared the annotation guidelines evaluated correctness.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to support question answering systems with genuine utility to users and to drive advances in natural language understanding.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset may be biased by focusing on Wikipedia as the evidence source and by excluding shorter queries and 'how to' questions through filtering heuristics.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to longer Google queries with Wikipedia pages in the top 5 results, excludes many shorter and 'how to' queries, and exhibits genuine ambiguity and variability in acceptable answers.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking, training, development, and testing of question answering systems; intended to provide large-scale end-to-end training data and evaluation for QA research.

name.evidence: We present the Natural Questions corpus, a question answering data set.

description.evidence: We present the Natural Questions corpus, a question answering data set. Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. An annotator is presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results, and annotates a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or marks null if no long/short answer is present.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Open-domain question answering (QA) is a benchmark task in natural language understanding (NLU), which has significant utility to users... We believe that, because a solution to NQ will have genuine utility, it is better equipped as a benchmark for NLU.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: We focus on Wikipedia as it is a very important source of factual information, and we believe that stylistically it is similar to other sources of factual information on the Web; however, like any data set there may be biases in this choice. Future data collection efforts may introduce shorter queries, 'how to' questions, or domains other than Wikipedia.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: All the questions in NQ are queries of 8 words or more... We run questions through the Google search engine and keep those where there is a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results... Future data collection efforts may introduce shorter queries, 'how to' questions, or domains other than Wikipedia... One clear finding in NQ is that for naturally occurring questions there is often genuine ambiguity in whether or not an answer is acceptable. There are also often a number of acceptable answers.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: Our goals are three-fold: 1) To provide large-scale end-to-end training data for the QA problem... We propose NQ as a new benchmark for research in QA... The public release consists of 307,373 training examples with single annotations; 7,830 examples with 5-way annotations for development data; and a further 7,842 examples with 5-way annotated sequestered as test data.
